---
title: "Comparison with other software"
description: "How GC–MS workflows resolve coelution, estimate component counts and use multiple samples."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

A coeluting compound contributes several ion traces with the same elution
profile. A single chromatogram already contains that information. Across a
batch, repeated spectra add evidence, while retention time, concentration
and peak shape can vary. The workflows below use different parts of this
information to separate components.

| Workflow | How components are resolved and counted | Background and noise | How samples are used | Access and source |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| GCMSprime | A peak-shape dictionary supplies candidate peaks. A penalized likelihood selects rank with nonnegative spectra and log-concave profiles. | The model fits a smooth baseline and estimates quasi-Poisson overdispersion by default. | Fits one sample directly or shares spectra across a batch, with disk-backed refinement. [Mathematical basis](algorithm.html) | Free, GPL open source. [Repository](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/GCMSprime) |
| GNPS/MSHub | Within each aligned retention-time group, NMF separates the matrix of peak integrals. Increases in explained sum of squares guide the component count. | Noise filtering and baseline correction precede factorization. | Uses multiple samples for deconvolution. GNPS can also use externally deconvoluted spectra for networking. [Aksenov et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-020-0700-3) | Free hosted workflow with a GNPS account. Public code under the repository's nonprofit-use licence. [Source](https://github.com/CCMS-UCSD/GNPS_Workflows/tree/master/mshub-gc) · [Licence](https://github.com/CCMS-UCSD/GNPS_Workflows/blob/733ed89372c3754a4c4d132319da5b4313c47288/LICENSE) |
| PARADISe | Fits candidate PARAFAC2 models within retention intervals. The published workflow includes reviewing the intervals and component counts. | Baseline and tail contributions can enter as factors in the least-squares model. | Fits multiple chromatograms with a common spectral mode and the PARAFAC2 cross-product constraint. [Johnsen et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2017.04.052) · [Protocol](https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.pex-2143/v1) | Free Community and paid Professional editions, distributed as applications. [Kromath](https://www.kromath.com/) |
| mzmine / ADAP-GC | Detected ion peaks define local windows. ADAP-GC 4.0 uses clustering-assisted multivariate curve resolution. | Peak detection and the selected module define preprocessing and separation. | Deconvolves individual chromatograms before batch feature alignment. [Smirnov et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.9b01424) · [mzmine guide](https://mzmine.github.io/mzmine_documentation/latest/module_docs/featdet_spectraldeconvolutiongc/spectraldeconvolutiongc.html) | Free mzmine Community licence for eligible academic users. ## What MSHub deconvolves

The GNPS implementation first groups aligned peaks by retention time.
For each group it forms a samples-by-ions matrix of peak integrals. Its
NMF gives a sample abundance and a mass spectrum for each component in
the group. The rank search compares successive improvements in explained
sum of squares. With no scan axis in its input, the factorization cannot
estimate a time-resolved elution profile for each component in each sample
or require its ions to follow one common profile. The NMF therefore has
no component profile on which to impose unimodality. [MSHub implementation](https://github.com/CCMS-UCSD/GNPS_Workflows/blob/733ed89372c3754a4c4d132319da5b4313c47288/mshub-gc/tools/mshub-gc/proc/preproc/peakdetect.py#L859-L995)

MSHub chooses rank automatically using fixed rules in the code. It rounds
the percentage of explained sum of squares, stops when adding a component
improves it by fewer than five percentage points, and has an additional
stopping rule for two consecutive equal improvements. In GCMSprime the
rank score uses a penalty on the number of components and occurrences,
evaluated with the selected noise model. [MSHub rank search](https://github.com/CCMS-UCSD/GNPS_Workflows/blob/733ed89372c3754a4c4d132319da5b4313c47288/mshub-gc/tools/mshub-gc/proc/preproc/peakdetect.py#L947-L995) · [GCMSprime rank criterion](algorithm.html)

The matrix has rank at most one for a single sample. Even with multiple
samples, two coeluting compounds with a fixed abundance ratio contribute
a rank-one matrix. If their sample abundance vectors are \(a\) and \(ca\)
and their spectra are \(s_1\) and \(s_2\), their summed contribution is
\(a(s_1 + c s_2)^\mathsf{T}\). Distinct profiles across scans can supply
separation evidence within a single run. GCMSprime retains this scan-level
information in the fit.

The public MSHub code switches to maximum-based spectrum extraction
below five samples. The GNPS guide recommends another deconvolution
workflow below about ten files. Networking and library search can then
use the spectra produced by that external tool. [MSHub sample-count check](https://github.com/CCMS-UCSD/GNPS_Workflows/blob/733ed89372c3754a4c4d132319da5b4313c47288/mshub-gc/tools/mshub-gc/proc/preproc/peakdetect.py#L744-L761) · [GNPS guide](https://ccms-ucsd.github.io/GNPSDocumentation/gc-ms-deconvolution/)

## What the coupled model changes

For each component in each sample, GCMSprime multiplies a single elution
profile by its shared mass spectrum. Every ion contributed by the component
therefore follows the same profile in that sample. The profiles may change
width, shift or tail across samples. Coupling enters the fit through the
shared spectrum, and the rank penalty counts that spectrum once, with a
separate amplitude for each occurrence. The objective and constraints are
given in the [algorithm article](algorithm.html).

PARAFAC uses a common profile for each component up to amplitude. PARAFAC2
allows different profiles but constrains their cross-products to be
constant across samples after separating the sample amplitudes. If a
broadening acid peak changes its normalized overlap with a neighbouring
compound, that constant cross-product assumption restricts the fit.
GCMSprime allows the overlap to vary while requiring each profile to be
log-concave. The [beer example](gcms-deconvolution.html#beer-volatiles-and-a-broad-acid-peak)
shows a broad, asymmetric acid peak in a single run.

With count noise, fitting the baseline together with the peaks lets the
model use the original intensity and its mean-dependent variance. A
background-subtracted trace is useful for display. The count model itself
uses the sum of background and peak contributions.

For measured runtime, compound recovery and memory layout, see the
[16-sample simulation and full-beer application](multisample.html).
